mcqs.question: What's the concrete design move behind "making this extensible without editing it," beyond just citing the Open/Closed Principle?
options: Find the seam where new behavior plugs in, add an extension point there (interface plus registry), and keep discovery separate from behavior
Rewrite the entire module using only static methods to avoid needing interfaces
Add a comment above the method warning future engineers not to edit it
Convert the method into a Singleton so it can only be modified in one place
mcqs.explanation: The actual move is identifying the seam and building a real extension point there, with discovery kept separate from behavior — a definition of OCP alone doesn't show this. Static-only rewrites, warning comments, and Singleton conversion don't create any extensibility at all.

mcqs.question: In the FormatterRegistry example, what has to change in FormatterRegistry itself to add a new PUSH format?
options: The format() method needs a new else-if branch for PUSH
Nothing in FormatterRegistry changes — adding PUSH is a new registry.register() call elsewhere
The MessageFormatter interface must be redefined to include a PUSH-specific method
The HashMap must be replaced with a different data structure to support PUSH
mcqs.explanation: The whole point of the registry-based extension point is that dispatch code never changes again — a new format is a new registration call, not an edit to FormatterRegistry. No new branch, interface redefinition, or data-structure change is needed.

mcqs.question: Two handlers are accidentally registered for the same input type. What's the recommended way to handle this?
options: Silently let the second registration overwrite the first, since last-registered-wins is always correct
Ignore it — duplicate registrations can never actually happen in practice
Make it an explicit design decision: fail loudly at registration time, or define an explicit priority/ordering rule, rather than leaving it to accidental registration order
Automatically merge both handlers' logic into a single combined handler at runtime
mcqs.explanation: The point is to decide this deliberately — either reject duplicate registrations outright or resolve them with an explicit priority rule — rather than leaving the outcome to whatever order registration happens to occur in. Assuming last-registered-wins is always correct, assuming it can't happen, and silently merging logic all skip making the actual decision.

mcqs.question: A feature has exactly two known variants with no signal of a third. What's the strongest recommendation for its extension point?
options: Build a fully generic, config-driven, auto-discovering plugin framework in case future variants appear
Skip creating any interface at all, and hardcode both variants inline permanently
Require every future variant to be added via a database migration, regardless of complexity
A simple interface with direct instantiation is enough; reserve registry, config-driven, or auto-discovery machinery for scenarios with real, ongoing growth
mcqs.explanation: Sizing the extension mechanism to the actual scenario means a plain interface is enough for two known variants — a full plugin framework here is speculative generality paying for flexibility nothing requires yet. Skipping an interface entirely under-engineers it, and mandating database migrations for every variant is an arbitrary, unrelated constraint.
